full_judgment:
K. Hossain J, : In this appeal the question of law involved, is, whether the appellant who is a government officer and therefore a public servant and was on deputation on foreign service basis to serve the Chittaranjan Cotton Mills Ltd, as Administrative Officer and was nominated by the company as a member of the Board of Trustees of the Chittaranjan Cotton Mills Employees Provident Fund Trust could be said to have ceased to be a public servant, so that any offence committed by him In his deputationary capacity is immune from requirement of sanction under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 2. The facts giving rise to the question of law are that, consequent on certain allegations made against the Chittarajan Cotton Mills Limited, Martial Law Order No. 104 of 1960 was promulgated by the Zonal Martial law Administrator of East Pakistan. Under this Martial law Order, the Provincial Government was empowered to appoint an Administrator, and take over the management of the Company. But the said Order clearly recited that the Company, shall continue to be a company under the Companies Act and that subject to the Martial law Order and the Rules made thereunder, the provisions of the Companies Act shall apply, The fluctuating details of the company's fortune need not be set out in extenso. All that is necessary to remember is that the company's control and management were in the hands of a Board of Directors, but in many respects the control rested in the hands of the Provincial Government. In the context of these facts, the appellant Mansur Ali Ahmed, an Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies, Chittagong, was placed at the disposal of the Chittaranjan Cotton Mills Limited, for appointment as Administrative Officer on foreign service basis. This was done on 19-5-69, The appellant was subsequently nominated en 5-6-69, by the company as one of its representatives to the Board of Trustees of the Employees Provident Fund Trust, and this was done as a sequel to the release of the predecessor of the appellant as Administrative Officer of the Company. While the appellant was so serving in the company on 31-12-1970, Respondent 2, a trustee of the Provident Fund Trust, lodged a complaint be-fore the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Dacca alleging that the appellant had forged a proceeding of a meeting of the Board of Trustees, purporting to authorise the transfer of Rs. 2,80,000/- from the Provident. Fund to the General Fund of the company, and sent a copy thereafter to the Mill's Bark. The complaint was one of the forgery and fraud. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate summoned the appellant under sections 420/511 and 464 of the Penal Code, and he surrendered to the court and obtained bail on 13-2-71, and the case was then transferred to a Magistrate, 1st Class, for disposal, The appellant then filed an application contending that his trial cannot proceed without the sanction of the Government under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Magistrate however proceeded with the trial and so the appellant moved the court of Sessions, Dacca for making a reference for quashing the proceedings for want of prior sanction of the Government for his prosecution. His further ground was that the offence alleged under section 420/511 of the Penal Code was a scheduled offence under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, and so exclusively cognizable by the Special Judge, appointed under the said Act. The Sessions Judge made a reference to the High Court for the acceptance, observing that sanction was necessary, as the appellant was a government servant and was alleged to have committed the offence in the purported discharge of his duties as such. He also held that the offence under section 420/511 P. C. was exclusively triable by Special Judge, and so the magistrate could not take cognizance of that offence, He recommended for quashing the proceedings. The learned Judge of the High court referring to a large number of decisions, took the view that, when the appellant was discharging his duties in the company, he was neither in pay of the Government, nor was he entrusted with the performance of any public duty, Though he was on deputation, yet while he was working in the company, he did not retain the status of a Government servant, nor was he clothed with any public duty. He was working as an employee of the company. It was also held that the appellant was nominated to the Board of Trustees as a "representative of the company", and he was not exercising any delegated function of the Government, nor his duties were immediately auxiliary to those of some one who was so armed. Their view was that the appellant did not come within the extended meaning of "public servant" given by Act III of 1967. The suddenness of this finding is the subject matter of this appeal. 

 3. Mr. Ansar Ali the learned counsel appearing for the appellant, has challenged the finding of the High Court Division on several grounds. Before dealing with the submissions of the learned counsel for the Appellant, we propose to deal with the principal question set out at the beginning of the appeal. The salient facts not in dispute may be set out, so that question of law can be appreciated in its true perspective. The appellant, an Assistant Registrar of the Cooperative Societies, is a Government servant, and his service were placed at the disposal of the company on foreign service basis. The Government's order conveyed to Registrar of Cooperative Societies, shows that the appellant was sent on deputation to serve the company and he was to get his grade pay plus deputation allowance at the rate of 20% over the grade pay. The medical facilities were allowed to him as per Government Rules. The residential accommodation would be provided by the company on payment of rent at the rate of 7-2/1 of his basic pay, The foreign employer will pay contribution towards pension, and leave salary of the officer concerned.  The appellant's period of deputation was of three years in the first instance. It is, therefore, manifest that the appellant was an officer of the Government, as he held the post of an Assistant Registrar of the Co-operative Societies. 

 4. The question then arises, that by going on deputation to a company at the order of the Government, whether the appellant temporarily ceased to be a Government servant for the period of his deputation. A large number of cases were reviewed by the High Court, but none of them is relevant to the point as none of them relates to the deputationary capacity of a Government servant. The cited authorities enunciated the test to be determined in judging an officer to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code, and they are not in dispute. A detailed discussion of these authorities is not called for. However, we would like to mention some of them. We think that the best enunciation of the principle is to be found in the case of G.A. Montario vs. The State of Ajmir, by the Supreme Court of India, reported in A.I,R, 1957 (S.C,) 113. The other three decisions we propose to deal, are Reg. vs. Remajirao Jirbaji, 12 Born. II C. R, 1(B) Nazamuddin vs. Queen Empress I, L.R. 28 Cal. 344 and Ahed Shah vs. Emperor A.I.R, 1918 Lah, 152, All these decisions have been considered in the case of Monterio by the Supreme Court of India. 

 5. The Bombay decision is the most important, as all other decisions have referred to the dictum laid down by West J. The person concerned in the Bombay case was as Izphatder i.e. a lessee of a village, who had undertaken to keep an account of its forest revenue and pay a certain proportion of it to the Government, keeping the remainder for himself. The question that arose for the consideration of the Court, was, whether he was an officer of the government. It was held that he was mere contractor bound by an engagement, but not by the term of his office or employment, to pay a certain proportion of the collection to the Government. The dictum of West J, is that the word "Officer" meant some parson employed to exercise to such extent arid in certain circumstances, a delegate of the Government. He may either himself he armed with some authority or representative character, or his duties were immediately auxiliary to those of someone who was so armed. 

 6. Nazamuddin's case is a decision of the Calcutta High Court, and the incumbent was a peon attached to the office of the Superintendent of the Sales Department in the district of Muzafferpore. He was convicted under section 161 of the Penal Code. Though the exact nature of his duties was not defined, 30 it was taken from the nature of his appointment, that his duty was to carry out the orders of his superior officer, the Superintendent, who was undoubtedly a public servant and so he was immediately auxiliary to the Superintendent, who was armed with the delegated function of the Government. He was held to be an officer the service and pay of Government in terms of S, 21 of the Penal Code. 

 7. Ahad Shah is a Lahore case and there the accused was managing proprietor of a firm, Ahed Shah and Mohammed Shah and Company, and was charged with the abetment of an offence under section 161 of the Penal Cede. There were three separate trials and each resulted in conviction of the accused. A defence taken was that the quarter Master's clerk to whom the accused was alleged to have abetted, was not a public servant, and so his conviction under section 161 P.C. was incompetent. It was held that the officer abetted was in the pay and service of the Government and was a non-commissioned officer and merely because he was working as a quarter master's clerk, he did not cease to be a public servant. An observation was made that it was not enough that a person should be in the pay or service of the government to constitute him a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code, but he must also be an officer. That expression is not, of course, to be restricted to its colloquial meaning of a Commissioned or non-commissioned officer, it means functionary or holder of some `officium' or office, The office may be one of the dignity or importance; it may equally be humble. The learned Judges of the Lahore High Court cited the dictum of West J. in their support. 

 8. In the case of Monterio, the incumbent was a metal examiner, also called chaser, in the Railway carriage workshops at Ajmer, and was held to be performing a public duty. The Supreme Court of India, first laid down that the test to be applied in judging a person an officer of the Government, is to see, whether he is in the service and pay of the Government, and whether he is entrusted with the performance of a public duty i. e. he has delegated to him the function of the Government, or in Any event performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is an officer of the Government and is therefore an officer of the Government within the meaning of section 21 (9) of the Penal Code. Holding the employee concerned a public servant, it was held that he was a Class III servant, employed as a examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops, under the Works Manager who was certainly an officer of the Government, and the duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to those of the Works Manager, who beside being an officer of the Government, was also armed with some authority or representative character qua the Government. The employee was found even on the narrow interpretation, within the dicta of West J. an officer in the service or pay of the Movement performing as such a public duty trusted to him by the Government. 

 9. The principles therefore are well recognised as to who is an officer of the Government and so a public servant. We are in full agreement with a dicta laid down by the Supreme Court of India set out above. That the appellant as an Assistant Registrar of Co-Operative Societies, Chittagong, was an officer of the Government, cannot and has not been disputed, and so he is a public servant under section 21 of the Penal Code. 

 10. A reference to the Bangladesh Constitution in this context is very pertinent. The constitution itself has defined the 'service of the Republic' and a 'public officer' when the constitution has defined and demarcated the status of the officer in service of the Republic, then all persons who come within the definition of the 'service' of the Republic whether high or low, are to be regarded as an officer of the Government or a Government servant, and whatever duties they will be discharging as servant, of the Republic assigned to them by the Government, either by rules or otherwise, shall be their duties as a public duly. 

 11. We now turn to the next limb of the question, as to the capacity of a Government officer, who is sent on deputation to a non-Government organisation. The relevant Rules are contained in Chapter 12 of the Bangladesh Service Jules (hereinafter referred to as Service Rules). Again, Rule 12 A of Bangladesh Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules 1960 as amended, may be looked into. Rule 98, Chapter 12, of the Service Rules inter alia, shows that a Government Servant can only be lent to the borrowing authority, who is a local authority or a public statutory Corporation, or for some other public reason, if the Government thinks that the duties to be performed after transfer are such, as should be rendered by a Government servant. The rules also provide, that the Government servant on deputation shall be in the cadre in which he was included in a substantive or officiating capacity, and may be given substantive or officiating promotion as the authority may decide. It is on record; that the appellant was to get his grade pay plus deputation allowance at the rate of 20% of his grade pay and medical facility as per rules of the Government. His leave was also to be governed by Service Rules. We get very significant indication about the status of a borrowed officer from Rule 12A of Efficiency and Discipline Rules 1960. It says, that when the service of a Government servant are lent to a borrowing authority, it shall have the power of placing the officer under suspension, and initiating proceedings against him, provided that the borrowing authority shall inform the landing authority of the circumstances leading to the order of his suspension or the commencement of the proceedings; and if the officer is a holder of class 1 service, then the prior approval of the Government is also necessary. The rule further says, that if the borrowing authority comes to a finding that any of the penalties specified in Rule 4 is to be imposed on the borrowed officer, it shall transmit the record of the proceeding to the lending authority, and the lending authority may pass such order as it deems necessary. No further details of the rules need be gone into, as a broad reference to the rules clearly indicates that on being lent to borrowing authority, whether it is a local authority or not, the borrowed officer continues to be a Government servant. 

 12. In this connection it may be observed, that Efficiency and Discipline Rules of 1960 along with some other rules have been repealed and replaced by the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1976. Though this rule is not strictly applicable to the facts of the case before us, still the definition of the 'Government servant' given in the Rule is a clear indication to the views we have expressed, 'Government servant' in the Rule has been defined to mean a person in the service of the Republic, and includes any such person on foreign service, or whose service are temporarily placed at the disposal of a local authority or other authority, or a foreign Government or Agency. No further discussion is called for. 

 13. Mr. Ansar Ali's contention is that the reasonings of the learned Judge of the High Court Division, that the officer on being lent to a borrowing authority, loses his status of a Government servant, when the borrowing authority is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, are contrary to and against the provisions of the Service Rules. We find, there is much substance in this contention. A Government servant if lent to a borrowing authority on foreign service basis, remains a Government servant. He does not lose his status or character of a Government servant. Whatever duly the officer discharges to the borrowing authority in his deputationary capacity, which under the rules the Government has thought it expedient for public reasons to be rendered by a Government servant, must be regarded as the duties of the officer on deputation. The mere fact that for the time being the Company, the borrowing authority, is paying the salary of borrowed officer from the company's fund does not detract him from his status of a Government servant. The Service Rules specifically provides for such payment of his salary by the borrowing authority. The payment is sanctioned by the Service Rules. His status as Government servant remains unaffected. 

 14. We may now refer to second ground of the learned Judges that the borrowing officer was not entrusted with the performance of any public duty. What is or is not a public duty is a question of fact, and will depend upon facts and circumstances of each case. We are here concerned with the duties of a Government servant lent to a borrowing authority. We have indicated earlier, that where a person, who is manifestly and undoubtedly a Government servant, in that lie is in the service of the Republic of Bangladesh, the duties performed by him and assigned to him either by rules framed by the Government, or by an order of the Government, or duties performed by him as assigned to him by his superior officer, are ipso facto public duties. All lawful duties of a Government servant, are public duties, by necessary implication the deputationary functions of the borrowed Government servant will be his duties. So long he is rendering his deputationary functions, his duties are to be regarded those of a borrowed Government servant. It is immaterial so far as the borrowed officer is concerned, as to the body or authority he is rendering the service. The criteria is his duly and his capacity as a borrowed officer, and not the body or authority where he is rendering his borrowed service. The duties of the appellant, a borrowed Government servant, within his deputationary function are to be regarded as a public duty. 

 15. Mr. Anser Ali has next argued that the finding of the learned judge of the High Court Division, that in any event the appellant as a trustee, was not acting as an administrative officer and so was not functioning within his deputationary capacity, is not correct in view of the fact that the appellant was in the Board of Trustees as a nominee of the Company, and the service of the appellant were placed by the Government at the disposal of the company. He was within his deputationary capacity even as a trustee of the Board. 

 16. Mr. Sultan Hussain Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney General, on behalf of the Government, has submitted that the Board of trustees is not an organ of the Company. It relates -to the provident fund of the employees of the Company, and the company has nothing to do with the fund, and so appellant was not functioning relating to the Company. The contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General does not bear the scrutiny of the facts on record. A reference to the nomination to the Board, by the Company and his letter of appointment by the Government, reveal that the services of the appellant was lent to the Company by the Government and the appellant was appointed in place of another Government servant, lent to discharge the function of an administrative officer of the company and whose service were withdrawn from the Company. He succeeded his predecessors, It is on record, that his predecessor was on the Board as no-mince of the Company in the capacity of an administrative officer. On the transfer of his predecessor both the post of administrative officer and a seat on Board became vacant. The appellant filled both the places as successor to his predecessor. The Company nominated the appellant as its nominee in his capacity as an administrative officer. He was rep-resenting the company in the Board. The Company had to contribute in the provident fund, the share of the employer, and so had very high stake involved in the said fund, Some representation in the Board is essential to protect the interest of the Company. The appellant's representation in the Board must be regarded as within his deputationary capacity. The fact that someone else could have been chosen, is not a true answer to the question qua the appellant. The question is not whether someone else could have been nominated to the Board, but whether the appellant could have been nominated, had lie net been the administrative officer of the Company. The answer is obvious. The Company was utilizing his service as a borrowed officer in the Board, for the purpose of the Company. We are unable to sustain the finding of the High Court Division. The appellant was a Government servant, and he continued as a Government servant in his deputationary capacity in the services of the Company, and the offence alleged against him, was committed in the purported exercise of his duty as a trustee, and within his deputationary capacity, and so he was entitled to the protection of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 17. The offence under section 420/511 alleged to have been committed by the appellant is in the schedule of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958, and is exclusively triable by a special Judge appointed under the said Act. The Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence under section 420/511 of the Penal Code.
